papers.title: Re. Emulating a Target Trial of Interventions Initiated During Pregnancy With Healthcare Databases: The Example of COVID-19 Vaccination.
papers.one_line: A letter showing that pairwise artificial censoring in sequential pregnancy emulations still requires inverse probability of censoring weights, and that the weights carry no information for the treated member of the pair, so the design loses precision without removing bias.
papers.what_was_done: A published extension of the target trial framework to point exposures in pregnancy proposes a series of trials indexed by gestational week, with treated and untreated individuals matched on baseline confounders and both members of a matched pair censored when either becomes non-adherent. Because untreated individuals can start treatment later while treated individuals cannot become untreated, the censoring event is triggered only by the untreated member. The letter works the structure through on a concrete example of COVID-19 vaccination and stillbirth, with baseline treatment affecting post-baseline treatment and stillbirth, and baseline treatment affecting post-baseline infection, which in turn affects both post-baseline treatment and stillbirth. Pairwise censoring balances non-adherence across arms, but the stated purpose of inverse probability of censoring weighting is to balance predictors of censoring within arms, not between them, so the weights are still needed. For the untreated member the weight conditions on post-baseline infection and removes bias; for the treated member the weight is predicted by the untreated partner's infection status and is uninformative. The result is lost precision on the treated side with the analytic burden unchanged, which the letter notes matters most in pregnancy research where sample sizes are limited.

future_research.gap: No implementation guidance exists for pairwise artificial censoring in sequential pregnancy emulations.
future_research.quote: We ask the authors to provide additional guidance for implementing this approach.

problems.evidence: Two analytic constructions are on the table for the same estimand, pairwise artificial censoring and censoring weights, and the letter concludes that the advantages of the first are unclear once the second is still required. Nothing in the published design obliged a demonstration that the choice changed the answer, and the disagreement surfaced only through correspondence. That is precisely a default adopted without evidence that it mattered.
problems.quote: Given that artificial censoring of the treated member of the pair reduces precision while still requiring investigators to address selection bias analytically, the advantages of this approach are unclear.

problems.evidence: The per-protocol effect recovered by censoring the pair is valid only under homogeneity of the treatment effect across predictors of censoring, an assumption the design does not test. Where homogeneity fails the reported contrast is a weighted effect among those whose partner remained adherent, not the per-protocol effect named in the protocol, and the two are reported in the same units.
problems.quote: Censoring the pair is sufficient to estimate a per-protocol effect if the treatment effect is homogeneous across predictors of censoring, but not otherwise.

problems.evidence: The construction spends sample twice: matching removes unmatched observations at baseline, and pairwise censoring then discards follow-up on treated individuals whose partner deviated, in exchange for no information gain on the treated side. In pregnancy databases, where the eligible cohort is already small, the effective sample after these two steps is not reported anywhere in the design.
problems.quote: No information would be gained among the treated, but precision would be lost due to artificial censoring.

problems.evidence: The design under discussion is a sequence of trials indexed by gestational week, with each individual eligible to enter at several weeks. The correspondence concentrates entirely on the censoring rule and never reaches the repeated participation the sequence creates or the calendar-time structure of vaccine availability across gestational weeks, which is left unexamined on both sides of the exchange.
problems.quote: The authors propose a series of target trials at each gestational week, matching treated and untreated individuals on baseline confounders.

papers.title: Invited Perspective: Risk of Bias Assessments, Target Trials, and the Strengths of Environmental Epidemiology.
papers.one_line: A perspective arguing that risk-of-bias domains in environmental epidemiology should be rebuilt around target trial concepts, while conceding that for exposures such as global climate change no individual-level treatment and therefore no time zero can be defined.
papers.what_was_done: A commentary on a systematic review of organophosphate and N-methyl carbamate insecticide exposure and sperm concentration, in which meta-analyses were prespecified to be stratified by risk-of-bias domain and restricted to low-risk studies. Studies commonly carried high risk of bias in the recruitment strategy and exposure ascertainment domains, and effect sizes fell substantially once only lower-bias studies were retained. Two domain criteria are challenged: recruitment strategy scored on population representativeness, and exposure ascertainment scored on measurement reliability, relevance of matrix and temporal stability. The argument against representativeness is structural: selection bias arises only when specific variables related to the exposure-outcome effect are selected on, so a demographically unrepresentative sample can be unbiased and a representative one biased. The proposed replacement is a common well-defined study entry point, with candidate anchors listed as developmental stage, chronological age, calendar year, start of employment or another anchor, and exposure measures restricted to the post-enrollment period. For exposure ascertainment the proposed overarching criterion is causal consistency, meaning a unit change in the measured exposure has the same effect regardless of how the change occurred. No numeric threshold, no effect-size bound and no decision rule is attached to any of these criteria; the whole proposal is an addition to a narrative rating scheme.

future_research.gap: Risk-of-bias criteria for the recruitment domain lack any requirement for a defined target population or a defined exposure timing anchor.
future_research.quote: Accordingly, future risk of bias assessments for the recruitment strategy domain could be refined by adding criteria for well-defined target populations and timing of exposure.

problems.evidence: Environmental exposures are exactly the case where the protocol component 'treatment strategy' has no referent. Measured concentrations of metabolites and breakdown products are not interventions, and the text concedes that for questions such as global climate change no individual-level treatment can be conceptualized at all, which removes time zero along with it. The proposal is to keep the framework anyway and use toxicokinetic modeling to guess what the value would have been in the right window, which substitutes a modeling assumption for a defined intervention.
problems.quote: Indeed, for some research questions such as effects of global climate change, it may be impossible to conceptualize individual-level treatments and therefore define appropriate time zero or other trial analog features.

problems.evidence: Causal consistency is named as the missing overarching criterion, and the reasons given are that identical measured concentrations can correspond to different timing, accumulation rate, metabolic conversion, developmental stage and coexposure mixtures. That is a statement that the equivalence class of exposure versions behind a single measured value is undefined. The only remedy offered is to stratify by setting, occupational against environmental and clinical against population, which is a coarse proxy chosen by convention rather than a procedure for constructing defensible equivalence classes.
problems.quote: There are a few ways that exposure measures may not represent consistent effects despite two individuals having similar measured concentrations.

problems.evidence: The anchor for time zero is offered as an open list: developmental stage, chronological age, calendar year, start of employment, or some other common anchor. Nothing in the text says how to choose among them, and the choice determines which exposure measurements count as post-enrollment and therefore which measurements enter the analysis at all. The recommendation stops at the observation that defining a common period may help, with no outcome-blind selection rule.
problems.quote: Any attempt to more clearly define a common period for real or potential exposure in the design of analyses may more naturally help protect studies from selection biases

problems.evidence: The framework is credited with producing less biased estimates than conventional analysis, and that credit is then used to justify writing target trial criteria into a risk-of-bias instrument, ROBINS-E, where meeting them lowers a study's rating. This converts framework membership into an assessment of assumption burden for an entire literature, in a field where the same text concedes the intervention analog often cannot be constructed.
problems.quote: Importantly, it has been shown that observational data analyzed under the target trial framework produce less biased estimates of effect than those analyzed conventionally.

problems.evidence: Exposure enters these analyses as a measured concentration treated as the causal exposure, and the domain rating checks only reliability, matrix relevance and temporal stability. The text points out that the measured quantity is frequently a metabolite, a breakdown product or another proxy of uncertain route, duration and intensity, so a perfectly reliable measurement can still be the wrong variable. Reliability metrics do not detect that failure, and the field carries the measured value forward as if it were the exposure itself.
problems.quote: Moreover, measurements taken in human populations may reflect exposures of uncertain routes, duration, or intensities, or they may exert their effects as complex mixtures, threatening the possibility of estimating consistent effects.

papers.title: On optimal timing of antenatal corticosteroids: time to reformulate the question.
papers.one_line: A commentary showing that the 24 hour to 7 day antenatal corticosteroid efficacy window, which came from a post-randomization subgroup analysis of a 287-woman trial and now drives obstetric guidelines, cannot be mapped to any randomizable intervention.
papers.what_was_done: The evidence base for antenatal corticosteroid timing rests on comparisons of subgroups defined by the treatment-to-delivery interval, a quantity that can only be observed at birth. In the original placebo-controlled trial 287 women were randomized, and the reduction in respiratory distress syndrome was largest in infants born below 32 weeks and between 24 hours and 7 days after trial entry, an absolute risk reduction of almost 30 percent. That subgroup finding was reproduced in later trials and observational studies and hardened into guidelines, including weekly repeat dosing, and into prediction models and biomarker tests built to identify who will deliver within 7 days. Two candidate mappings from interval to intervention are worked through. Randomizing the interval at the time of administration requires manipulating delivery itself through induction or tocolysis, which excludes spontaneous deliveries and raises ethical objections. Randomizing at presentation and manipulating the time of treatment requires knowing the time of delivery in advance, which is unavailable without a perfect prediction model. The proposed replacement is a multi-arm target trial of adaptive regimes that initiate treatment when a periodically updated risk prediction crosses a threshold, with 30 percent and 40 percent given as example thresholds; the number of strategies makes the sample size requirement extreme.

future_research.gap: The proposed threshold-based adaptive timing regimes have not been evaluated, and the protocol is offered as guidance for future database emulations rather than as a completed analysis.
future_research.quote: Even if, for this or any other reason, this target trial would not be conducted, its protocol still provides important guidance for future observational studies that may attempt to emulate it using large retrospective databases

problems.evidence: The treatment-to-delivery interval is a protocol component that is unobservable at the decision point and knowable only at birth. What the literature estimates is therefore not a noisy version of the intended timing effect; it is a contrast between groups defined by a post-randomization event, which no trial could assign. Guidelines recommending the 24 hour to 7 day window were built on that data-defined quantity, so a whole clinical recommendation rests on an estimand that has no interventional counterpart.
problems.quote: It may seem obvious that such intervals are not randomizable interventions, but merely retrospective observations
problems.locator: Which hypothetical target trial do previous subgroup comparisons try to emulate?

problems.evidence: An observed interval of, say, three days is compatible with different treatment versions: a woman treated early whose labor progressed slowly, a woman treated late after induction, a woman given tocolysis. These are pooled into one exposure level with no procedure for deciding which versions belong together. The consequence is stated directly: identical observed intervals correspond to different received interventions, so the contrast has no single interpretation.
problems.quote: two patients may be identical in terms of their observed interval, yet differ with respect to the timing and type of their received intervention(s)

problems.evidence: The 24 hour to 7 day window was not specified in advance; it is the interval within which the observed risk reduction was largest in a subgroup analysis of the original trial. Once selected on the outcome it became the design constant for later trials, observational studies and guidelines, and prediction models were then built to hit it. This is the outcome-driven time-window selection the registry entry describes, propagated across a literature for five decades without an outcome-blind procedure ever being applied.
problems.quote: Such subgroup analysis of the first placebo-controlled randomized controlled trial indicated that a one to seven day interval between ACS administration and birth resulted in the lowest rates of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

problems.evidence: The only formulation of the timing question that survives the analysis is a dynamic regime: treat when a periodically updated risk prediction crosses a threshold, with effect modifiers such as gestational age at each decision point folded into the rule. Identification of such regimes requires the risk prediction to be updated at decision times that are themselves driven by the patient's evolving state, and the practical barrier named is that comparing the many candidate thresholds needs an extremely large sample. No estimator or identification result is supplied for the continuous-time version of the problem.
problems.quote: Due to the large number of treatment strategies to be compared, actually conducting such a trial would require an extremely large sample size.

problems.evidence: The diagnosis is that the mismatch is at the level of the scientific target, not at the level of confounding control, and that decades of adjustment for confounding by indication in interval-based observational studies addressed the wrong layer. There is no accounting that separates that scientific-target mismatch from residual confounding or estimation error, and the failure was invisible precisely because the reported analyses looked like standard adjusted comparisons.
problems.quote: we may need to reformulate the scientific question of interest altogether

papers.title: Start with the Target Trial Protocol, Then Follow the Roadmap for Causal Inference.
papers.one_line: A commentary accepting the target trial protocol as a starting point but arguing that its assignment-procedure component covers only conditional exchangeability, and proposing a nine-step Roadmap that forces every identification assumption, the estimator choice and the interpretation to be stated separately.
papers.what_was_done: The motivating statistic is a review of a random sample of 75 observational studies of cardiovascular disease, diabetes or osteoporosis in which 95 percent had at least one avoidable methodological issue known to incur bias. Against that background the target trial protocol is accepted as a way to state the question in familiar language, but its claim that design and analysis then flow naturally is rejected. The nine Roadmap steps are laid out: specify the question, specify a causal model, define counterfactuals, describe what is measured, state and evaluate identification assumptions, choose a statistical estimand, choose an estimator on its statistical properties, run sensitivity analyses, and interpret. The specific criticisms of the protocol are that its assignment-procedure component concentrates on conditional exchangeability while missingness and data support are left implicit, that pairing emulation with matching can change the target population and is often less efficient, and that alternative identification strategies such as difference-in-differences sit outside the protocol's frame. Estimator selection is required to rest on bias and variance and to avoid unrealistic functional form assumptions, with doubly robust estimators such as targeted maximum likelihood as the usual destination and finite-sample simulations on the empirical confounder distribution with blinded outcomes as the selection device. Interpretation is graded on a published hierarchy in which claiming to have emulated a trial requires four conditions including a zero causal gap and an intervention that could have been randomized.

problems.evidence: Step 5 makes delineating every identification assumption a required output rather than a discretionary paragraph, and Step 8 attaches sensitivity analysis to the specific assumptions that remain untestable, with the explicit warning that the gap between adjusted and unadjusted estimates says nothing about whether confounding was handled. What is not closed is the dashboard itself: there is no fixed set of fields, no requirement to label an assumption diagnosable or undiagnosable, and no threshold at which a stated causal gap makes a claim unreportable.
problems.quote: the Roadmap explicitly requires researchers to delineate all necessary identification assumptions every time they aim to estimate a causal effect

problems.evidence: Step 7 replaces the free choice of estimator with a selection procedure: candidate algorithms, including different Super Learner libraries and sample-splitting schemes, are compared on finite-sample simulations built from the study's own confounder distribution with outcomes blinded, and the comparison is written into the analysis plan before estimation. That is a concrete answer to the demand that a study show its estimator choice was defensible. It does not close the entry: the procedure is a recommendation in a commentary, no criterion says when the differences between candidates are large enough to report, and nothing requires the losing candidates to be published.
problems.quote: Candidate algorithms should be compared using finite sample simulations reflecting the challenges in the real data.
problems.locator: RED LIGHT [CHOOSE AN ESTIMATOR]; GREEN LIGHT [ESTIMATE!]

problems.evidence: The concern raised is that completing the protocol components invites over-interpretation, because the output is still an observational study carrying multiple biases including intractable confounding. The remedy proposed is a separate interpretation step with an explicit hierarchy, which is only necessary because the emulation label by itself carries no information about the assumption burden. A field that needed to add a four-condition test before a study may claim to have emulated a trial is a field where the label was doing that work unearned.
problems.quote: we still have an observational study, subject to multiple potential biases, including intractable confounding

problems.evidence: The causal gap names one of the components the registry entry asks to be separated: the distance between the statistical parameter that is estimable and the causal parameter that was wanted. Steps 1 to 7 are then assigned to estimation error and identification separately, so two layers are pulled apart rather than reported as one number. What remains undecomposed is the earlier loss: the distance between the scientific question and the target trial protocol that was written for it, and the further loss when that protocol is compromised to fit the data. Those two are absorbed into Step 1 and never quantified.
problems.quote: Without identification, the true value of the statistical parameter that we will estimate from the observed data will not be equivalent to our wished-for causal parameter; in other words, there will be a so-called causal gap.

problems.evidence: Machine learning is placed where it belongs, at the functional form problem inside estimation, and is fenced by the requirement that it be incorporated so that 95 percent confidence intervals remain valid. The identification question is handled in a separate step, and the interpretation step insists that a nonzero causal gap leaves an association regardless of how flexible the estimator was. What is not closed is the practice: the entry concerns studies that present flexible estimation as a remedy for identification failure, and a commentary recommending a different ordering does not stop them.
problems.quote: machine learning may help minimize bias due to reliance on misspecified parametric regressions, but must be incorporated in a manner that yields valid 95% confidence intervals
problems.locator: RED LIGHT [CHOOSE AN ESTIMATOR]; GREEN LIGHT [ESTIMATE!]

problems.evidence: Data support is named as one of the assumptions that the protocol's assignment-procedure component leaves implicit and whose violation produces severely misleading inference. The Roadmap's answer is to require the assumption to be stated, not to require that the unsupported covariate histories be identified and named, so a study can satisfy the step with a sentence and no diagnostic at all.
problems.quote: Doing so can minimize the potential for severely misleading inferences arising from violations of assumptions related to missingness or data support, among others.

papers.title: Should multiple imputation be stratified by exposure group when estimating causal effects via outcome regression in observational studies?
papers.one_line: A 252-scenario simulation showing that the missing-data handling step alone moves the estimated average causal effect by up to 35.6 percent relative bias, with imputation stratified by exposure group the least biased when the smaller exposure group is large enough.
papers.what_was_done: Seven approaches to missing data were compared for estimating an average causal effect by outcome regression without interactions: complete-case analysis, multiple imputation with no interactions, four imputation models carrying exposure interactions, and imputation run separately within exposure groups. The design was built on the Victorian Adolescent Health Cohort Study, 1,943 participants of whom 1,000 were female, with an analytical sample of 953 females, 8.8 percent exposed to weekly cannabis use in adolescence and 72.8 percent complete records. A total of 252 scenarios crossed three exposure prevalences, three missingness mechanisms and seven outcome generation models, each with 2,000 simulated datasets. In the scenario where missingness depended only on exposure, every method was approximately unbiased with a maximum of plus or minus 3.3 percent relative bias. Where missingness depended on exposure, a strong confounder and their interaction, imputation with no interactions reached 35.6 percent relative bias under a strong negative exposure-confounder interaction and minus 8.2 percent under a strong positive one, while stratified imputation and correctly specified interaction imputation stayed below 3.8 percent. Bias fell as exposure prevalence rose. In the secondary simulations stratified imputation was approximately unbiased at total sample sizes of 1,300 or more but was the most biased method with the largest mean squared error when the total was 500 and the exposed group held about 50 observations. In the real case study all seven methods gave similar estimates.

future_research.gap: The comparison does not cover binary outcomes or continuous confounders.
future_research.quote: Still, our study does not cover all possible scenarios, and further investigations considering other scenarios would be worthwhile, specifically considering settings with a binary outcome or continuous confounders

future_research.gap: Stratified imputation has no defined form for a continuous exposure.
future_research.quote: Third, it is unclear how the approach should be applied in the continuous exposure setting.

problems.evidence: Nothing in the estimand or the identification assumptions changes across the seven methods; only the nuisance step for missing data does, and the estimate moves from approximately unbiased to 35.6 percent relative bias. Complete-case analysis and imputation without interactions are the two defaults in current practice and are the two that fail. No study reporting an average causal effect from outcome regression is required to show that this choice did not drive its answer.
problems.quote: The relative bias given by MI-NI in missingness scenario (iii) was up to 35.6% in the strong negative interaction outcome scenario

problems.evidence: The recommended method breaks on exactly the samples that database emulations produce after eligibility restriction: with 500 observations total and roughly 50 in the exposed group, stratified imputation was biased and had the largest mean squared error of all seven approaches. Since the case study itself had 8.8 percent exposed among 953, the crossing point is inside the range of ordinary applied studies, and the diagnostic that matters is the count in the smallest exposure group rather than the size of the source cohort.
problems.quote: when the total sample size was 500 (the size of exposed group was around 50), the results indicated that MI-EG was biased and yielded the largest MSE among all approaches

problems.evidence: The operational guidance that comes out of 252 scenarios is a narrative rule: avoid the stratified approach when the smallest exposure group is relatively small. The one number attached, 50 observations, comes from a single simulation cell, and nothing states the count at which an analysis should not proceed. A reader with 120 exposed individuals has no rule to apply.
problems.quote: Additionally, our recommendation is to avoid using the MI-EG approach when the smallest exposure group is relatively small

problems.evidence: Which of the three missingness mechanisms holds is the single determinant of whether the default analysis is unbiased or 35.6 percent off, and the three are distinguished only by arrows in a missingness directed acyclic graph, not by anything estimable from the data at hand. A published emulation reports its missing-data method next to its confounding adjustment with no marker that one rests on an undiagnosable assumption.
problems.quote: The estimates given by all methods were approximately unbiased in missingness scenario (i) (missingness only depended on the exposure, maximum ± 3.3% relative bias)

papers.title: Augmenting control arms with real-world data for cancer trials: Hybrid control arm methods and considerations.
papers.one_line: A simulation of hybrid control arms in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer where dynamic borrowing lifted power from 74.1 percent to 88.5 percent under no residual bias but let type I error reach 0.097 to 0.13, and where the tuning parameter that sets the trade-off has to be chosen from residual bias estimated in other diseases.
papers.what_was_done: A frequentist two-step borrowing method was proposed and compared with a commensurate prior, a test-then-pool procedure and a static power prior, using parameters from a completed randomized trial in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. Under the target scenario of an experimental hazard ratio of 0.78 and no residual bias between the real-world and randomized controls, power was 88.5 percent for the commensurate prior, 88.6 percent for test-then-pool, 88.5 percent for the two-step model and 90.2 percent for a power prior with the power parameter fixed at 0.6, against 74.1 percent for a model that borrows nothing. The static power prior always borrowed 60 percent of external events regardless of similarity and its type I error was not capped; the dynamic methods capped maximum type I error at 0.13 for test-then-pool, 0.12 for the commensurate prior and 0.097 for the two-step model, with inflation peaking at moderate residual bias near a hazard ratio of 1.2 and falling as the discrepancy grew. The effective number of borrowed external events fell as residual bias grew and as the experimental effect weakened. Selecting the tuning parameter requires an estimate of expected residual bias, and the source proposed for it is prior replication exercises: eleven advanced non-small cell lung cancer trials whose control arms were emulated in an electronic record database, nine of which had residual bias hazard ratios between 0.96 and 1.10 for overall survival, and a separate set of fifteen trials across tumor types with residual bias hazard ratios mostly between 0.66 and 1.09. The illustrative benefit calculation was 225 fewer enrolled patients, a readout four months earlier and a 2:1 randomization ratio.

future_research.gap: Borrowing methods do not yet incorporate covariate balancing weights, including weights for post-baseline treatment patterns.
future_research.quote: it will be important to develop methods for incorporating covariate balancing weights into borrowing methods, including weights to balance post-baseline characteristics and treatment patterns such as differences in treatment duration and subsequent therapies

future_research.gap: No criteria exist for deciding early in enrollment whether borrowing will be possible, leaving a trial exposed to being underpowered if the interim assessment refuses the external data.
future_research.quote: In order to mitigate these risks, additional research is needed to develop and assess decision criteria that can be applied early in a trial's enrollment.

problems.evidence: The design that a regulator would review has an operating characteristic that cannot be stated in advance: the amount of borrowing is a function of how similar the data turn out to be, and maximum type I error across the plausible bias range reached 0.097 to 0.13 for the dynamic methods. There is no threshold for acceptable residual confounding, no bound on tolerable type I error inflation, and the recommended route is early discussion with the agency rather than a stated standard.
problems.quote: the exact amount of borrowing cannot be pre-specified and is dependent on data similarity

problems.evidence: Fitness for purpose is the gate that decides whether external data enter the control arm at all, and it is assessed narratively: whether trial eligibility criteria including biomarker and genomic requirements can be applied, whether covariate balance on prognostic characteristics is achievable, and whether endpoints, index dates and follow-up align. No cut point appears for any of the three, and a study that fails them has no defined stopping rule; the statistical borrowing step is offered as the protection instead.
problems.quote: Prior to borrowing information from an external source, it is critical to assess whether the external data are fit for purpose.

problems.evidence: The tuning parameter for a future breast cancer trial is to be set from residual bias measured by replicating control arms in lung cancer and in a mixed set of tumor types, on the grounds that the eligibility criteria are similar. Nothing licenses that transfer: the reported spread in the fifteen-trial set runs from 0.66 to 1.09, and one of the eleven lung cancer replications missed because the trial population was enriched for a biomarker not accounted for in the alignment steps. Successful replication of past control arms is being extrapolated to a new question with no theory that says when it carries.
problems.quote: Such evaluations provide a sense of how much residual bias may be plausible and relevant when selecting the value of tuning parameters and assessing the overall suitability of a hybrid design for a future cancer trials with similar I/E criteria.

problems.evidence: Replication is put to work as a measurement rather than a verdict: the control arm of a completed trial is rebuilt from the same data source and the discrepancy is reported as a residual bias hazard ratio, which then feeds a tuning parameter with a stated effect on power and type I error. That is the calibrated comparison the entry asks for, on one estimand. What it does not close is the general case: the calibration is a single overall survival hazard ratio, it says nothing about other endpoints or estimands, and the headline reporting of past replication exercises still travels as the count of trials that agreed.
problems.quote: by replicating the control arms of recently completed studies (ie, following steps 1–3 and then comparing outcomes with the randomized control) in the same disease area and trial setting, and with the same external data source, it may be possible to develop empirical evidence for how much residual bias might be expected

problems.evidence: The external cohort is aligned to the trial population by eligibility application and covariate balancing, then its events are borrowed under a similarity model, so a sampling assumption and a confounding assumption are compounded inside one weight. The gap is acknowledged from the other side: methods for combining covariate balancing weights with borrowing, including weights for post-baseline treatment duration and subsequent therapies, are named as still to be developed.
problems.quote: we think there may be opportunities for simpler solutions that retain a clear causal estimand

problems.evidence: Index date alignment between the trial and the external cohort is listed as one of the fitness conditions, alongside endpoint definitions and follow-up time, and is then left as an alignment exercise with no rule. Where historical patients are admitted to enlarge the cohort, the correction offered is censoring all events after the trial follow-up duration at a pre-specified maximum, a second time-grid decision taken with the outcome data in hand.
problems.quote: and to align endpoint definitions, index dates, and follow-up time

papers.title: ASO Author Reflections: Real-World Effectiveness of Prehabilitation Before Colorectal Cancer Surgery: The Value of an Emulated Target Trial Design.
papers.one_line: A reflections piece on a single-center emulated target trial of 251 colorectal surgery patients reporting a number needed to treat of 4.2 and a 55 percent lower comprehensive complication score, and stating that registry databases lack the clinical variables needed to repeat it.
papers.what_was_done: A single-center emulated target trial compared a multimodal prehabilitation program with usual care in patients undergoing elective colorectal cancer surgery who were aged 65 or older, or younger than 65 with ASA class III or IV. The cohort was 251 patients, 128 receiving usual care and 123 receiving prehabilitation. In the intention-to-treat analysis the number needed to treat to avoid one or more complications in one person was 4.2 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 2.6 to 10. The comprehensive complication score was 55 percent lower with prehabilitation, 95 percent confidence interval minus 71 percent to minus 32 percent, and length of stay fell 33 percent, 95 percent confidence interval minus 44 percent to minus 18 percent, from 7 days to 5 days. There was no effect on readmissions, which were already few. The comparator is usual care with no specification of its content, and the prehabilitation program is described only as multimodal. The stated reason for turning to observational data is that the existing randomized trials of prehabilitation ran under ideal circumstances in selected patients and disagreed among themselves, ranging from meaningful gains in functional walking capacity to no effect on postoperative outcomes.

future_research.gap: Extension beyond a single center has not been done and the registry databases needed for it lack frailty scores, granular complication scores and patient-reported outcomes.
future_research.quote: The methodology used (ETT) in this study could be an example for further multicenter studies.

problems.evidence: Prehabilitation is a multimodal behavioral and exercise program delivered by a care team, not a dispensed product, and neither its components, its dose, nor the unit to which it is assigned is defined anywhere in the report. The stated obstacle to repeating the design elsewhere is not confounding but that databases do not carry the variables that would define who was eligible for the program and what they received.
problems.quote: to be able to use (large) clinical registration databases in future ETTs on the effect of prehabilitation and other complex interventions

problems.evidence: The fitness verdict on clinical registration databases is delivered as a wish list: they should carry frailty scores, more specific clinical outcomes such as the comprehensive complication score, and patient-reported outcomes. There is no threshold at which their absence would stop an emulation, and the study just completed proceeded without any of the three being available in registry form, using single-center records instead.
problems.quote: these databases should incorporate more clinical predictor variables (e.g., frailty score)

problems.evidence: The result is positioned against the prior randomized trials as a directional label, additional evidence that prehabilitation works in daily practice, with no comparison of estimands. The randomized trials reported functional walking capacity and postoperative outcomes; the emulation reports a number needed to treat of 4.2, a 55 percent reduction in a complication score and a 2-day shorter stay. Nothing aligns the contrasts, the populations or the outcome scales, so the agreement claim rests on sign alone.
problems.quote: this study provides the first preliminary evidence that prehabilitation does not only improve outcomes in a controlled study setting but also in daily clinical practice

problems.evidence: The analytic cohort is 251 patients split 128 to 123 after eligibility restriction to older or high-ASA patients at a single center, and the imprecision shows in the intention-to-treat number needed to treat, whose interval runs from 2.6 to 10, close to a fourfold spread. This is the scale an emulation reaches once a complex intervention forces reliance on records that actually document the program.
problems.quote: The ETT included 251 patients: 128 in the usual care group and 123 patients in the prehabilitation group.

problems.evidence: Both arms are named by label rather than by content. A multimodal prehabilitation program covers an unspecified mixture of exercise, nutrition and psychological components at unspecified intensity, and usual care covers whatever the center did otherwise, which changed over the accrual period as the program was introduced. No procedure appears for deciding which delivered versions of either arm count as the same treatment.
problems.quote: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of a multimodal prehabilitation program compared with usual care on perioperative outcomes in patients undergoing elective colorectal surgery with a higher postoperative complication risk, using an emulated target trial (ETT) design.

papers.title: Medication-Wide Association Study Plus (MWAS+): A Proof of Concept Study on Drug Repurposing.
papers.one_line: A three-step drug repurposing pipeline ending in a target trial emulation of 251,692 matched pairs in Veterans Health Administration data that reported an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.97 for statin initiation and dementia and treated that as confirmation of the hypothesis.
papers.what_was_done: Step 1 screened ten drugs in a case-control analysis drawn from a Veterans Health Administration cohort of 4,045,269, restricted to 3,295,711 with at least ten years of history, containing 199,368 dementia cases matched five controls to one case on age, sex, race and ethnicity for 1,196,226 records. Cumulative dose was split into deciles and odds ratios computed against non-users with a Bonferroni threshold of 0.005; atorvastatin gave an odds ratio of 0.94 with a dose gradient and duloxetine 0.85 without one. Step 2 was a narrative literature review of statin mechanism. Step 3 emulated a target trial: four annual enrollments from 2002 to 2005 among patients with hyperlipidemia, statin initiators matched one to one with non-initiators whose index date was the date of a random qualifying prescription, propensity scores from a logistic model over demographics, income, area, year, disease duration, comorbidities, body mass index, blood pressure, serum glucose and lipids, giving 251,692 matched pairs. The adjusted hazard ratio for incident dementia was 0.97 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.96 to 0.99 and p equal to 0.0007, with 13.0 percent of patients having an event in both arms and mean time to event 8.8 years on statin against 8.5 years off. A subgroup of statins other than simvastatin and lovastatin, 6,980 patients, gave 0.89 with an interval of 0.83 to 0.95, adjusted for propensity score rather than matched. Prior observational studies had reported reductions of 15 to 35 percent and randomized trials none.

future_research.gap: The new-user design ignores cumulative exposure, which the screening step suggested is the dimension that matters.
future_research.quote: In future studies, we plan to use marginal structural modeling to count for the difference in cumulative exposure.

problems.evidence: The framework label carries the causal claim here. A propensity-matched new-user cohort with the same 13.0 percent event rate in both arms is described as emulating randomization, and the entitlement to a causal reading is asserted from the design name rather than from any stated assumption or diagnostic. No unmeasured confounding analysis, positivity check or negative control appears anywhere in the pipeline.
problems.quote: Using a target trial framework and target trial design can potentially allow us to make inferences on causal relationships.

problems.evidence: Agreement with randomized evidence is declared as a direction rather than measured. The randomized trials found no effect; the emulation found a hazard ratio of 0.97 with an interval of 0.96 to 0.99, which is statistically significant and clinically negligible, and other observational studies reported 15 to 35 percent reductions. Calling 0.97 aligned with the trials and not with the observational literature is a verbal classification of a point estimate, with no comparison of estimands, follow-up windows or populations behind it.
problems.quote: The target trial design in Aim 3 is intended to mimic a randomized controlled trial and indeed produced results that were more aligned with the randomized controlled trial than with other observational studies.

problems.evidence: The treatment arm pools every statin into one strategy while the same discussion concedes that the agents differ in blood brain barrier permeability and potency, which is the mechanism the hypothesis runs through. The pooled estimate is 0.97 and the subgroup excluding simvastatin and lovastatin is 0.89, so the equivalence class chosen by the analysis moves the estimate by more than the effect it reports. No procedure defined that class; it followed from what the formulary dispensed.
problems.quote: In addition, different statins have somewhat different properties including blood brain barrier permeability and potency.

problems.evidence: The comparator arm was drawn from patients with hyperlipidemia, a population in which most patients go on to receive a statin, and this is given as the explicit reason for choosing an intention-to-treat style new-user analysis over an on-protocol one. Follow-up averages 8.5 to 8.8 years, over which the comparator converges toward treatment, and the reported hazard ratio of 0.97 is the attenuated contrast that convergence produces. Nothing in the analysis quantifies how much of the null result the convergence accounts for.
problems.quote: because statin prescription is common in patients with hyperlipidemia and most patients would receive a statin, an on-protocol design would result in a much shorter follow up in the control group than in the treatment

problems.evidence: A source cohort of 4,045,269 shrinks to 251,692 matched pairs after eligibility and matching, and the subgroup carrying the actual screening signal, the statins other than simvastatin and lovastatin, contains 6,980 patients. That subgroup could not be propensity matched at all and was handled by covariate adjustment instead, so the largest number in the study and the number the conclusion depends on differ by nearly three orders of magnitude.
problems.quote: the number of patients with other statin prescriptions including Atorvastatin was relatively small

problems.evidence: The screening step and the mechanistic review both point at cumulative exposure, with the dose-response gradient across deciles as the reason for pursuing statins at all. The emulation then estimates an initiation contrast and reports it as a hazard ratio of 0.97, a quantity that answers a different question from the one that generated the hypothesis, and the mismatch is recorded only in the plans for future work.
problems.quote: In step 3, we used a new user design, which does not consider the cumulative exposure.

papers.title: Approaches to Selecting "Time Zero" in External Control Arms with Multiple Potential Entry Points: A Simulation Study of 8 Approaches.
papers.one_line: A simulation of 8 rules for setting time zero in an external control arm finds five viable, rules out last eligible line and censoring survival at progression, and reports that without standardized mortality ratio weighting every rule except propensity matching was substantially biased.
papers.what_was_done: Eight rules for choosing time zero were compared where external control patients are eligible at several successive lines of therapy: first eligible line, last eligible line, all lines with the patient contributing multiple records, all lines with survival censored at progression, a single random eligible line, repeated random sampling minimizing mean absolute error, repeated random sampling minimizing root mean squared error, and propensity score matching on the closest line. The setting was oncology, motivated by a comparison of axicabtagene ciloleucel in follicular lymphoma against a pooled electronic record and trial control cohort, where the single-arm study required at least 2 prior lines and its patients had a mean of 3.6 and a maximum of 9. The base case was constructed so that external controls entered at earlier lines than intervention patients, biasing the comparison against the intervention. Without standardized mortality ratio weighting, every method except propensity matching showed substantial bias for progression-free survival, which the report reads as evidence that a confounding-control step is required whatever the time-zero rule. With weighting applied, bias in the Cox hazard ratio ranged from 0.005 to 0.013 across the viable methods and coverage from 94.1 percent to 96.0 percent. Last eligible line was biased in all outcomes and all-lines-with-censoring was biased for overall survival in every scenario, so both were dropped. First eligible line had the largest 95th percentile error of the viable methods. Roughly 18 scenario analyses varying sample size, follow-up length, covariate relationships, survival model and number of treatment lines left the ranking unchanged.

future_research.gap: The comparison rests entirely on simulated data and has not been run on real cohorts where a randomized benchmark exists.
future_research.quote: For these reasons, we would encourage further work, ideally in real data sets such as large randomized controlled trials from which samples could be taken and the methods compared.

problems.evidence: Eight candidate time-zero rules are enumerated and evaluated against a known truth, and two are eliminated on performance rather than on argument, which is more than the field usually has. What is not supplied is an outcome-blind selection rule: five methods survive with bias in the Cox hazard ratio between 0.005 and 0.013 and nothing distinguishes them, so the choice is handed back to the analyst on grounds of interpretability, power and compatibility with other steps. An analyst who tries several and reports one is not detectable under this guidance.
problems.quote: In selecting between the viable methods, analysts should consider the context of their analysis and justify the approach selected.

problems.evidence: Censoring overall survival at progression is treated in practice as a way to keep follow-up clean, and the simulation shows what it actually does: patients who have not progressed are increasingly upweighted to stand in for those who have, and the quantity estimated becomes effectiveness in a population where progression cannot occur. Estimates deviated substantially from the benchmark in every scenario except the one where survival was exogenous to the disease process. The alternative named is to treat progression as a competing event, which is a different estimand again, and no default exists.
problems.quote: By artificially censoring patients on progression, we essentially changed the target of estimation.

problems.evidence: The reporting package recommended alongside a time-zero choice is exactly the one the registry entry describes as insufficient: histograms of weights, effective sample sizes and a statement of overlap between studies. None of these names which prior-line histories in the external cohort have no counterpart in the single-arm trial, which is the structural problem when the trial required at least 2 prior lines and controls entered at earlier lines by construction.
problems.quote: a demonstration of why each characteristic is selected for balancing, the degree of overlap between studies, histograms of weights, and effective sample sizes

problems.evidence: Five of eight methods perform indistinguishably and no superior approach is identifiable, so the reported estimate depends on a choice the analyst makes for reasons of taste and explanation. Nothing in the design requires the alternatives to be run and shown, and the very small differences that do appear are attributed to simulation artifact rather than to method properties.
problems.quote: Our main findings demonstrate that several methods for generating estimates in time-to-event outcomes have similar (low) levels of bias and precision, with limited evidence for a single superior approach.

problems.evidence: The all-lines rule is repeated participation in its purest form: one patient contributes several records and a single death is attributed to more than one treatment line. The simulation reports that this did not bias point estimates and often gave numerically better ones, which is a real piece of evidence on the efficiency side. It leaves the rest of the entry open: coverage for overall survival was noted as lower for most methods, no clustering correction is described, and the calendar-time structure that produces earlier lines in the external cohort and later lines in the trial is handled by weighting rather than examined.
problems.quote: Using multiple records per patient, in which death could be attributed to multiple treatment lines in the same patient, did not result in bias, and indeed frequently produced numerically superior estimates.

problems.evidence: The estimate is transported from an external control cohort to the population of a single-arm trial by standardized mortality ratio weighting, and that weighting is what makes the time-zero rules work at all: unweighted, all but one were substantially biased. The sampling assumptions the weighting requires and the confounding assumptions the covariate set requires are handled by the same step and reported as one weighted estimate, with no separate accounting of either.
problems.quote: A key finding was that application of SMR weighting was essential in supporting the methods used for the selection of time zero

papers.title: Comment on: Effect of bariatric surgery on cancer risk: results from an emulated target trial using population-based data.
papers.one_line: A correspondence from the Swedish Obese Subjects study group showing that a published emulated target trial misdescribed the design of the controlled study it invoked as a comparator, and reporting the actual controlled estimate for colorectal cancer as an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.89.
papers.what_was_done: A population-based emulated target trial of bariatric surgery and cancer risk discussed conflicting evidence on colorectal cancer and cited a report from the Swedish Obese Subjects study in support. The correspondence from that study group makes two factual corrections. First, the citation implies the Swedish study used standardized incidence ratios comparing surgical patients with the general population, when in fact it ran a prospective controlled design with a matched obese comparison group. Second, the specific report cited concerns female cancer and does not address colorectal cancer at all. The group then supplies the estimate that does exist: in a report dedicated to colorectal cancer incidence after bariatric surgery within the prospective controlled study, the adjusted hazard ratio with surgery was 0.89 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.62 to 1.29 and a p value of 0.551, that is, no evidence of an effect. Both parties agree that an adequately matched obese control group is the decisive design feature for this question.

problems.evidence: The emulation placed its colorectal cancer result against prior evidence by narrative citation and got the comparator's design wrong, attributing to it a general-population standardized incidence ratio when it was a matched controlled cohort. A comparison of estimands would have made the error impossible, because the two contrasts are not the same quantity. Instead the agreement or disagreement was asserted at the level of a label and stood until the original investigators wrote in.
problems.quote: However, by citing a SOS report in the Discussion erroneously, this implies that the method used in the SOS study is that of standardized incidence ratios (comparing patients who had bariatric surgery with the general population), which is not the case.

problems.evidence: The controlled comparison that exists for this exact question returns an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.89 with an interval from 0.62 to 1.29 for colorectal cancer, while the emulation reported a reduction in cancer risk overall. Nothing in the field says whether an emulation that matches controlled evidence on aggregate cancer incidence should be trusted on a site-specific outcome where the controlled evidence is null, and the correspondence supplies no such principle either.
problems.quote: we found no evidence that colorectal cancer is affected by bariatric surgery

problems.evidence: The design feature both sides treat as decisive is whether the comparison group is an adequately matched obese cohort, which is a substantive question about exchangeability and not something the emulation label answers. That a published emulation could misstate the design of the controlled study it was contrasting itself with, and have the error caught only by the investigators who ran it, shows how little scrutiny the framework label attracts on its own.
problems.quote: We fully agree with the authors that the inclusion of an adequately matched, obese control group is of the utmost importance when assessing the effects of bariatric surgery.

papers.title: Temporal Trends in Clinical Evidence of 5-Year Survival Within Electronic Health Records Among Patients With Early-Stage Colon Cancer Managed With Laparoscopy-Assisted Colectomy vs Open Colectomy.
papers.one_line: An emulation of the COST colectomy trial in 943 electronic record patients over 2006 to 2017 that detected significant calendar-time trends in both treatment assignment and survival and, after calendar stratification with cotraining, reported a 5-year risk difference of minus 0.007.
papers.what_was_done: The Clinical Outcomes of Surgical Therapy trial of laparoscopy-assisted against open colectomy, run from 1994 to 2001 with 839 patients and individual-level data obtained through Project Data Sphere, was emulated in Mass General Brigham records for colectomies performed from 2006 to 2017 with follow-up to 2020. Colon cancer status came from an unsupervised multimodal automated phenotyping algorithm validated against 171 labels, and stage came from a natural language processing extraction. After applying the trial's eligibility criteria the cohort was 943 patients, 518 laparoscopic and 425 open. The emulation cohort differed from the trial: stage I prevalence 19 percent against 38 percent, colon adhesion 7 percent against 18 percent, sigmoid tumors 45 percent against 38 percent. Adoption of laparoscopy rose from 81 of 231 patients in 2006 to 2009, to 132 of 277 in 2010 to 2013, to 305 of 435 in 2014 to 2017. Tests for calendar trend were significant for treatment assignment, chi-square 60.3, and for overall survival, chi-square 137.2. After calendar stratification with cotraining across strata, the 5-year risk difference was minus 0.007 with a 95 percent confidence interval of minus 0.070 to 0.057, matching the trial's noninferiority conclusion. Absolute survival was higher than in the trial by 0.074 for open colectomy, 95 percent confidence interval 0.011 to 0.131, and by 0.061 for laparoscopy, minus 0.001 to 0.122, and rose across the three periods.

future_research.gap: The temporal adjustment strategy has not been validated on a second trial emulation.
future_research.quote: Validation of the analysis on a similar RCT is limited by data availability.

future_research.gap: Indication bias in the early adoption period remains unaddressed because the variables that would explain it are not extractable.
future_research.quote: The information regarding the indication mechanism might be contained in detailed radiological characteristics but not extractable for our analysis.

problems.evidence: The trial being emulated was completed in 2001 and its individual-level data, protocol and report sheets were in hand before the emulation was designed, including the noninferiority result the emulation went on to reproduce. This is stated plainly as a limitation, and the only mitigation named is a reference to prespecifying an analysis plan, which was not done here. Inference proceeds as if the target trial and its adjustment strategy had been fixed in advance.
problems.quote: The knowledge of findings from the target trial might be associated with the design of the EHR emulation.

problems.evidence: Calendar-time confounding is measured rather than assumed away: chi-square 60.3 for the calendar contribution to treatment assignment and 137.2 for its contribution to survival, with laparoscopy adoption rising from 35 percent to 70 percent across the span. The correction offered is stratification by calendar period with cotraining so that some data-selected associations may change over time, and it moved the answer, since the unadjusted benchmark analyses differ. This addresses only the calendar-time half of the entry; the emulation enters each patient once at first colectomy, so the repeated participation that sequential designs create is not touched.
problems.quote: When both treatment and response patterns shift over time, the calendar year becomes a confounding factor.

problems.evidence: The comparison with the trial is carried out on the estimand scale rather than as an agreement label: the treatment effect is reported as a 5-year risk difference of minus 0.007 with an interval, and the arm-specific survival levels are compared to the trial with their own intervals, 0.074 higher for open colectomy and 0.061 higher for laparoscopy. That separates a matching contrast from a shifted level, which a binary replication verdict would hide. It does not close the entry: the headline framing is still that the emulation reached the same conclusion as the trial, and no calibration statistic or prespecified agreement margin is defined.
problems.quote: the estimated 5-year survival rates based on the EHR emulation analyses were 0.074 higher (95% CI, 0.011-0.131) for the OC group and 0.061 higher (95% CI, –0.001 to 0.122) for the LAC group

problems.evidence: One of the trial's eligibility criteria, tumor size, could not be applied at all because the value is absent from the record text, and patients with missing stage were excluded rather than assessed. The resulting cohort contains 19 percent stage I against the trial's 38 percent and 7 percent adhesions against 18 percent, differences that are consistent with criteria having been silently satisfied by absence of documentation. Nothing in the design distinguishes an unrecorded criterion from a met one.
problems.quote: We were unable to replicate the criterion for tumor size owing to the absence of exact information in EHR medical reports.

problems.evidence: Disease status, stage and tumor location all enter as algorithm outputs: a phenotyping algorithm checked against 171 labels, a natural language processing stage extractor, and a rule-based tumor location extractor whose accuracy could not be assessed because no reference standard existed. All three then function as error-free classifications in eligibility and adjustment, and no measurement error correction or sensitivity analysis is carried through to the risk difference of minus 0.007.
problems.quote: We developed a rule-based extraction for tumor location, but validation was infeasible because of the lack of criterion standard information.

problems.evidence: A health system registry yields 943 eligible patients, and the calendar adjustment that the analysis requires then splits them into strata of 231, 277 and 435. The number of periods was chosen as a compromise between allowing change points and keeping estimation stable, which is a sample-size constraint deciding the resolution of the confounding adjustment rather than the science deciding it.
problems.quote: We split the 12 years into 3 periods to allow for multiple change points while maintaining a reasonable sample size within each temporal period to ensure stable estimation.
problems.locator: EHR Cohort for Emulating the RCT

papers.title: Bias of time-varying exposure effects due to time-varying covariate measurement strategies.
papers.one_line: A simulation of 150,000 individuals in which the true 5-year risk difference is zero shows inverse probability weighting recovering it exactly under monthly covariate measurement, returning 29 percent under 6-monthly measurement, and flipping to minus 14 percent when covariates are measured only when exposure switches.
papers.what_was_done: A target trial was simulated in which participants are randomized at baseline to a monthly prescription or to none, followed for 60 months, with no causal exposure effect built in, alongside observational studies sharing the data-generating mechanism but differing only in when time-varying covariates are measured. Sample size was 150,000 per study, roughly 40 percent of subjects switched exposure level by the end of follow-up, and inverse probability weighting was used with last observation carried forward between measurements. The trial gave a 5-year event risk of 31 percent in both arms and a risk difference of zero. Without any covariate measurement the observational risk difference was 49 percent, 64 percent against 15 percent. Monthly measurement reproduced the trial exactly, a risk difference of zero. Six-monthly measurement gave 29 percent, 50 percent against 21 percent, and the bias rose with interval length to a plateau near 35 percent at 5 years and 20 percent at 2 years; measuring only at baseline recovered about 15 percentage points relative to no measurement at all. Measuring covariates only when exposure switched flipped the sign to minus 14 percent, 27 percent against 41 percent, and the mixed design of switch-triggered plus 6-monthly gave minus 5 percent, reaching minus 18 percent at an interval near 30 months. Averaging over 5,000 runs at sizes 150,000, 10,000 and 1,000 reproduced these values; at size 100 all designs including full measurement showed small-sample bias.

future_research.gap: No rule exists for how long a measurement interval a given study can tolerate.
future_research.quote: The maximum interval length that is sufficient to yield negligible bias will depend on the rates at which treatments and covariates can change

problems.evidence: The measurement process is drawn into the causal structure rather than left as an imputation nuisance: the observed covariate is represented as a separate node with arrows from prior and current covariates and from prior and current exposure, which makes it a collider on the path from exposure to outcome, so conditioning on it opens that path. This explains the sign flip from plus 29 percent under fixed intervals to minus 14 percent under switch-triggered measurement, and it is a genuine advance over treating gaps as missing data. What is not closed is the estimator: no method is offered that recovers the effect when measurement is exposure-driven, and the only advice is to measure more often.
problems.quote: Together with LOCF, these measurement designs introduced a form of differential misclassification, which may result in bias even in the absence of confounding.

problems.evidence: Observation driven by the treatment process is exactly the case the entry names as unresolved, and here it is shown to be worse than uninformative: bias reverses sign relative to fixed-interval designs, reaching minus 18 percent at an interval near 30 months, so the direction of the reported effect depends on the observation rule. The setting simulated is deliberately simple, a single binary covariate, no censoring before administrative end and static rather than dynamic strategies, so the continuous-time dynamic-regime version of the problem is not even attempted.
problems.quote: We additionally showed that bias might arise in settings where decisions to measure are driven by observed values of the time‐varying exposure.

problems.evidence: The measurement interval is a time-grid choice made at the design stage, and it moves the 5-year risk difference across a range of roughly 53 percentage points, from plus 35 percent to minus 18 percent, around a truth of zero. No outcome-blind rule selects it: the guidance is that shorter is safer and that the tolerable length depends on unobserved switching and covariate change rates. A study that reports its grid without justification is indistinguishable from one that chose it after seeing results.
problems.quote: we caution against implementing measurement designs with long intervals between measurements, particularly when the impact of the design choices are poorly understood

problems.evidence: The covariate is binary and its carried-forward value is used as if it were the true current value, which is where the damage happens: the misclassification is differential because whether the value is refreshed depends on exposure. The simulated covariate is perfectly measured when it is measured at all, so the entire distortion, up to 35 percent in one direction and 18 percent in the other, comes from treating a stale binary variable as a current one.
problems.quote: For the analysis, it was assumed that covariates remain constant in periods of no measurement.

problems.evidence: Whether a database can answer a time-varying exposure question at all turns on how often its covariates are refreshed, and that property is knowable in advance. No threshold exists: the reported dependence is on unobservable switching and covariate change rates, so a study with 6-monthly laboratory values has no rule that would stop it, even though this simulation puts that design 29 percentage points from the truth. The cited real studies of antidepressants and hip fracture used exactly the switch-triggered plus 6-monthly design that produced the sign flip here.
problems.quote: The maximum length required will depend on the rates at which treatments and covariates change, with higher rates requiring shorter measurement intervals.
